facts.fact: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12-35.
FRs were inspired by the US Bill of Rights and the UDHR.
Part III is called the Magna Carta of India.
The original Constitution had seven FRs; now there are six.
The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Part III.
The Right to Property is now a legal right under Article 300A (Part XII), available to any person.
FRs are justiciable — enforceable in courts.
FRs are not absolute; reasonable restrictions may be imposed.
Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are available only to citizens.
Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22 and 25-28 are available to all persons, including foreigners.
The right to vote and to be elected is a constitutional/legal right, not a Fundamental Right.
Rights are claims of citizens against the State (UPSC 2017).
One implication of equality is the absence of privileges (UPSC 2017).
Rule of law means limitation of powers, equality before law and liberty and civil rights (UPSC 2018).
Judicial review is the power of courts to pronounce on the constitutionality of laws and executive orders.
FRs are justiciable and mostly negative; DPSPs are non-justiciable and positive.
Article 12 defines 'State' to include the Union and state governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities.
Article 12 covers any body exercising public functions, so that all are accountable for FRs.
Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with FRs void — the basis of judicial review.
Article 13(1) voids pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with FRs.
Article 13(2) bars the State from making laws that take away or abridge FRs.
Article 13(3) defines 'law' to include ordinances, orders, by-laws, rules, regulations and notifications.
Article 13 protects FRs against laws; Article 368 is the separate power to amend the Constitution.
Article 14 combines equality before law (British) and equal protection of laws (American).
A law giving the executive unguided, uncontrolled discretion violates Article 14.
Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Article 15 also covers access to shops, hotels, wells and public places.
Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children.
Article 15(4), added by the 1st Amendment (1951), allows special provisions for backward classes and SC/ST.
Article 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005) allows reservation in educational institutions including private ones, except minority institutions.
Articles 15(6) and 16(6) (103rd Amendment, 2019) provide up to 10% EWS reservation.
Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment.
Under Article 16(3) Parliament may prescribe residence as a condition for certain jobs.
Article 16(4) permits reservation for backward classes not adequately represented in services.
Article 16(4A) (77th Amendment, 1995) allows reservation in promotion for SC/ST.
Article 16(4B) (81st Amendment, 2000) allows carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies.
Article 16(5) allows offices of religious institutions to be reserved for persons of that religion.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence.
The Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.
'Untouchability' is not defined in the Constitution.
Protection against untouchability falls under the Right to Equality (UPSC 2020).
Article 18 abolishes titles except military and academic distinctions.
A citizen may not accept a foreign title without the President's consent.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles (Balaji Raghavan, 1996).
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession.
The seventh freedom, 19(1)(f) property, was deleted by the 44th Amendment.
The freedom of assembly is to assemble peaceably and without arms.
The freedom of association includes forming co-operative societies (97th Amendment).
Freedom of the press is part of freedom of speech and expression (Romesh Thappar, 1950).
Article 19(2) grounds include sovereignty and integrity, security, friendly relations, public order, decency, contempt, defamation and incitement.
The 1st Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations and incitement; the 16th (1963) added sovereignty and integrity.
Article 20(1) bars ex-post-facto criminal laws.
Article 20(2) bars double jeopardy.
Article 20(3) bars self-incrimination.
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty except by procedure established by law.
The right to privacy is protected under Article 21 (Puttaswamy, 2017).
Privacy is intrinsic to Article 21 and the freedoms of Part III (UPSC 2018).
The right to marry a person of one's choice is protected by Article 21 (UPSC 2019).
Article 21 has been read to include a clean environment and health.
Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) gives free and compulsory education to children of 6-14 years.
The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 gives effect to Article 21A.
Under Article 22 an arrested person must be informed of the grounds and may consult a lawyer of choice.
An arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time.
Article 22 arrest safeguards do not apply to enemy aliens or preventive detainees.
Preventive detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board report.
Preventive detention laws include the PDA 1950, MISA 1971, COFEPOSA 1974 and NSA 1980.
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour.
Article 23 protects against private persons too, and economic compulsion counts as forced labour.
Compulsory service for public purposes, such as military service, is an exception to Article 23.
Article 24 bars children below 14 from factories, mines and hazardous work.
Article 24 does not prohibit employment of children in harmless work.
The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005 set up national and state child-rights commissions.
Right against Exploitation covers trafficking/forced labour and child labour, not untouchability or minorities (UPSC 2017).
Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion.
Article 25 is available to citizens and non-citizens.
Forced conversion is not protected by Article 25.
Under Article 25 the State may regulate secular activities and undertake social reform.
Carrying a kirpan is part of the Sikh religion; 'Hindus' in Article 25 includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists.
Article 26 gives religious denominations freedom to manage their religious affairs and own property.
A religious denomination has common beliefs, a common organisation and a distinct name.
Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion.
Article 28 bars religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State.
Religious instruction is permitted in State-administered institutions established under a trust.
In State-recognised or State-aided institutions religious instruction is permitted on a voluntary basis.
Article 29 protects any section of citizens' distinct language, script or culture.
Article 29 protects religious and linguistic minorities and the majority too.
Admission to State-aided institutions cannot be denied on religion, race, caste or language.
Article 30 lets religious and linguistic minorities establish and administer educational institutions.
The State cannot discriminate against minority institutions in granting aid.
Article 30 is for minorities only, while Article 29 is for any section of citizens.
Article 31 was omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Article 31A saves five kinds of laws (acquisition of estates etc.) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
The five 31A categories are estates, State management of property, amalgamation of corporations, directors/shareholders rights, and mining leases.
Article 31B protects Ninth Schedule laws from FR challenge.
Ninth Schedule laws added after 24 April 1973 can be reviewed (I.R. Coelho, 2007).
Article 31C saves laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
The second part of 31C (barring courts from asking whether a law gives effect to the policy) was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati.
The 42nd Amendment's extension of 31C to all DPSPs was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).
Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Article 32 can be invoked only for violation of Fundamental Rights.
Parliament may empower other courts to issue writs (Article 32(3)).
Enforcement of FRs can be suspended during a National Emergency under Article 359.
Before 1950 only the High Courts of Bombay, Madras and Calcutta could issue writs.
High Court writ power under Article 226 is wider in scope (FRs and other legal rights); the Supreme Court's covers a larger territory.
The five writs are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
Habeas Corpus can be issued against public authorities and private individuals.
Habeas Corpus does not lie where detention is lawful, for contempt, or by a competent court.
Mandamus ('we command') directs a public official to perform a legal duty.
Mandamus does not lie against private persons, for discretionary duties, or against the President or Governors.
Prohibition lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, not administrative or legislative ones.
Certiorari is both preventive and curative and lies also against administrative authorities.
Quo Warranto tests a claim to a substantive public office; any interested person may seek it.
Quo Warranto does not lie for ministerial or private offices.
Article 33 lets Parliament restrict FRs of armed forces, police, paramilitary and intelligence agencies.
Article 34 restricts FRs while martial law is in force and allows Parliament to indemnify officers.
'Martial law' is not defined in the Constitution.
Martial law affects only FRs and suspends ordinary courts; a National Emergency affects FRs, Centre-state relations and more, while courts continue.
Martial law is imposed in specific areas to restore law and order; a National Emergency is for war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
Article 35 gives Parliament alone (not state legislatures) power to make laws on certain FRs.
Article 35 matters: residence (16(3)), other courts' writs (32(3)), forces (33), martial-law indemnity (34), untouchability (17), trafficking (23).
Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 during a National Emergency.
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even in an Emergency (44th Amendment).
FRs are the foundation of political democracy, protect minorities, strengthen secularism and check governmental power.
Criticisms: excessive limitations, no socio-economic rights, lack of clarity, no permanency, suspension in Emergency, expensive remedy, preventive detention.
A.K. Gopalan (1950) upheld preventive detention, treated Article 22 as self-contained and preferred procedure established by law over due process.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) held the right to travel abroad is part of Article 21 and the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable.
ADM Jabalpur (1976) denied habeas corpus during the Emergency; Justice H.R. Khanna dissented.
ADM Jabalpur was overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).
Puttaswamy (2017) was decided by a nine-judge bench.
Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity, passive euthanasia and living wills.
Shankari Prasad (1951) held Parliament can amend FRs; an amendment is not 'law' under Article 13(2).
Golaknath (1967) held Parliament cannot amend FRs to abridge them.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, laid down the basic structure doctrine and overruled Golaknath.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368(4) and (5); judicial review is basic structure.
Mumbai Kamgar Sabha (1976), through Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, laid the foundation of PIL.
Sunil Batra (1978) held prisoners keep their Article 21 rights.
Hussainara Khatoon (1979) held speedy trial is part of Article 21.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) ordered release and rehabilitation of bonded labourers.
Olga Tellis (1985) held the right to livelihood is part of the right to life.
M.C. Mehta (1986) laid down absolute liability for hazardous industries.
Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation with a 50% ceiling and creamy-layer exclusion.
Indra Sawhney held caste can be the basis to identify backward classes under 16(4).
Unnikrishnan v. State of A.P. (1993) made education up to 14 years a right under Article 21.
Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd Amendment's 10% EWS quota.
Romesh Thappar (1950) held press freedom is part of free speech.
Champakam Dorairajan (1951) struck down communal quotas, leading the 1st Amendment to add 15(4).
Vishaka (1997) laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace.
NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons as the third gender.
Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act.
Shayara Bano (2017) held instant triple talaq unconstitutional under Article 14.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 IPC.
Joseph Shine (2018) struck down Section 497 IPC (adultery).
The Sabarimala judgment (2018) allowed women of all ages to enter the temple.
Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) protected students who stood but did not sing the national anthem.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati functions separately from 1 January 2019.
